clue.text: Lacklustre send-up of Shakespeare

indicators.note: in a down clue a send-up literally sends the word upwards, so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: Shakespeare is known as the Bard of Avon

explanation.surface: A dull parody of Shakespeare's plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Something drab is dull and colourless, lacking any shine or interest.

clue.text: Country work that's also part recreation

definitions.text: Country work that's also part recreation

parts.note: surface reading: labour on a farm, such as tending sheep
setter's reading: a poem, play or symphony depicting rural life, which re-creates the countryside in art

explanation.surface: Farm labour that doubles as a leisure pursuit.
explanation.walkthrough: Read recreation as re-creation: an artistic work that re-creates rural life is a piece of this genre.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary or musical work idealising shepherds and rural life is given this name, from the Latin for shepherd.

clue.text: Twenty pence contribution? That's kind!

indicators.note: the phrase makes a contribution of some of its letters, so the solution sits inside it

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone thanks a donor for a small coin given to charity.
explanation.definitionFit: Type and kind are synonyms meaning a sort, category or class of thing.

clue.text: Robert Oppenheimer's first association with a songbird

parts.note: Bob is the usual short form of Robert

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the physicist's surname is wanted

parts.note: initial of the surname
a link is a connection or association

explanation.surface: A biographical note on the physicist Robert Oppenheimer's earliest link to birdwatching.
explanation.definitionFit: The bobolink is a North American songbird of the blackbird family, named for its bubbling call.

clue.text: Deceive with terrific talk

parts.note: to con is to trick or deceive
fab is slang short for fabulous

explanation.surface: A smooth talker deceives people with brilliant patter.
explanation.definitionFit: A confab is an informal chat or discussion, short for confabulation.

clue.text: I am England's new star

indicators.note: a new version of the phrase means its letters are rearranged into something fresh

parts.note: all ten letters used as fodder

explanation.surface: A boastful new England football star announces himself as the country's hope.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining fodder to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The leading man is the principal male actor in a film or play, its star.

clue.text: German writer introducing German article about Old English

indicators.note: the first piece is put in front, leading in the pieces that follow

parts.note: standard abbreviation for German
standard abbreviation for Old English
the definite article

explanation.surface: A German author's book opens with a piece on Old English.
explanation.walkthrough: The order is loose: the article sits after the Old English, so 'about' is read as merely joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, author of Faust, is Germany's most celebrated writer.

clue.text: Advance slowly and cautiously, or steal quietly away

indicators.note: sending the musical soft sign away removes it from the word for steal

parts.note: to pinch is to steal
p is piano, the musical marking for quiet

explanation.surface: A thief creeps forward carefully, then slips off silently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steal quietly away' reads as one sneaky action, but it is steal minus quietly.
explanation.definitionFit: To inch along is to creep forward by tiny amounts, carefully and gradually.

clue.text: Set for scan? Why?

parts.note: to scan is to read through
the letter Y is pronounced like the word why

explanation.surface: Someone prepared for a hospital scan asks what it is for.
explanation.walkthrough: Y and 'why' sound the same, a common crossword equivalence.
explanation.definitionFit: Being set, as in 'all set to go', means prepared and willing to start.

clue.text: Yoko has no news about being solo

parts.note: Yoko Ono, artist and widow of John Lennon

indicators.note: the words are moved about, so their letters change places

parts.note: six letters used as fodder

explanation.surface: Yoko Ono hears nothing about a solo career.
explanation.definitionFit: Being solo means acting alone, without help or company from anyone else.

clue.text: Before start of race, punter is richer

indicators.note: says the start-of-race word follows the punter, with the punter put in front

parts.note: a punter is one who bets
"They're off!" marks the start of a horse race

explanation.surface: A gambler who places a bet before the race begins is in profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start of race' looks like a first-letter instruction, but it means the word heard as the horses leave.
explanation.definitionFit: To be better off is to be in a more prosperous or wealthier position.

clue.text: Get rid of 500 yen

parts.note: D is 500 in Roman numerals
a yen is a craving or itch

explanation.surface: Dumping five hundred units of Japanese currency.
explanation.walkthrough: Yen looks like money next to the number, but it means a longing.
explanation.definitionFit: To ditch something is to discard or abandon it, informally throwing it away.

clue.text: Swiss city takes in one Italian artist

parts.note: Bern is the Swiss capital
taken as written
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A Swiss city welcomes an Italian painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes in' looks like a container, but nothing fits inside the city; the city simply takes the word in and the one.
explanation.definitionFit: Gian Lorenzo Bernini was the great Italian Baroque sculptor and architect of seventeenth-century Rome.

clue.text: Prince finally among the creme de la creme. Harry?

indicators.note: one piece placed among the others sits inside them

parts.note: the creme de la creme is the very best

indicators.note: only the closing letter of the royal title is kept

parts.note: last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Is Prince Harry finally counted among the elite?
explanation.walkthrough: Harry looks like the prince's name but is a verb, to harass.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry is to harass persistently, and to beset is to trouble or assail on all sides.

clue.text: Heartlessness and senselessness about olfactory offensiveness

indicators.note: one word goes round about the other, enclosing it

parts.note: inanity is silliness or lack of sense
hum is British slang for a bad smell

explanation.surface: A rant about cruelty, stupidity and terrible smells.
explanation.walkthrough: A hum, in British slang, is a nasty pong, so the stink goes inside the foolishness.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhumanity is cruelty and lack of compassion, the condition of having no heart.

clue.text: Crazy blunders involving knucklehead

indicators.note: the mistakes involve, or wrap round, the other piece

parts.note: a boner is a blunder or howler
read as knuckle's head, its opening letter

explanation.surface: Mad mistakes made by a dimwit.
explanation.walkthrough: Knucklehead looks like an insult for a fool, but it splits into knuckle and head.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonkers is informal British slang meaning mad or crazy.

clue.text: Port in northern Massachusetts, beer in southern Massachusetts, initially

indicators.note: the drink is put in among the selected letters
the opening letters of the two place words are wanted

parts.note: the first letter of each word
ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: A guide to New England: a harbour up north, a brew down south.
explanation.definitionFit: Salem is a historic harbour city on the Massachusetts coast north of Boston, famous for its witch trials.

clue.text: Airy-fairy?

parts.note: surface reading: vague, impractical or fanciful
setter's reading: a fairy creature of the air, a spirit of that element

explanation.walkthrough: Airy-fairy normally describes woolly thinking; split it literally and it is a spirit made of air.
explanation.definitionFit: In folklore a sylph is an elemental spirit of the air; the word also describes a slender, graceful woman.

clue.text: Not quite a royal family

indicators.note: not quite the whole word, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: a king is a royal

explanation.surface: A family that falls just short of royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Kin are one's relatives, the people related by blood.

clue.text: Worthies revealing why schoolchildren are innumerate?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, split as two words: the pupils have not learned their times tables

explanation.surface: Dignitaries discuss why pupils cannot do arithmetic.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer after the second letter for the joke: pupils with no multiplication tables cannot count.
explanation.definitionFit: Notables are prominent, distinguished people, the worthies of a town or community.

clue.text: Exemplary poser

definitions.meaning: first meaning: perfect, fit to be copied
second meaning: one who poses for an artist or photographer

explanation.surface: A perfect show-off.
explanation.walkthrough: Poser suggests a poseur or a puzzle, but it means someone who strikes poses.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means ideal, worth imitating; as a noun, a person who sits for artists.

clue.text: Wendy's family pets

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the family name of Wendy in Peter Pan

explanation.surface: The animals kept by Wendy's household.
explanation.walkthrough: In J M Barrie's Peter Pan, Wendy, John and Michael belong to this London family.
explanation.definitionFit: Pets are favourites or beloved people, and darlings are dearly loved ones.

clue.text: Transport me with large hamper

parts.note: a tram is a form of transport
taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Carry me along with a big picnic basket.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamper looks like a basket but is a verb, to hinder.
explanation.definitionFit: To trammel is to restrict or impede someone's freedom of movement or action.

clue.text: Failed to move away from home

indicators.note: getting the letters to move puts them in a different order

parts.note: six letters used as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone who never managed to leave home.
explanation.definitionFit: Afield means at a distance, abroad, far from where one usually lives.

clue.text: Well-heeled or well-oiled? Such a question is unfair
Paddy has so much French spirit

parts.note: tant is French for so much
rum is a spirit

explanation.surface: An Irishman named Paddy has plenty of French brandy.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddy looks like a man's name; in British English a paddy is a fit of temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a paddy is British slang for having a fit of bad temper or rage.

clue.text: Shoot a descendant

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a young plant cutting used for grafting
second meaning: an heir of a noble family

explanation.surface: An instruction to fire at someone's heir.
explanation.definitionFit: A gardener's graft cutting and a young member of a distinguished family share this word.

clue.text: Silly ass holding head of pin for pinheads

indicators.note: the donkey word holds the other letter inside it
silly suggests nonsense, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: A foolish donkey clutching a pin, with fools all round.
explanation.definitionFit: Saps and pinheads are both informal words for stupid, gullible people.

clue.text: Colour that's in, in inn in France

indicators.note: the second in tells us one piece sits in the other

parts.note: auberge is French for an inn
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tongue-twisting description of a fashionable shade at a French hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: The string of 'in's is deliberate: the first is the letters, the second the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Aubergine names the dark purple colour of the vegetable's skin, the eggplant.

clue.text: It's 5.5 yards, going round one way

indicators.note: the measure goes round the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: a rod is an old unit of length, five and a half yards
a means one

explanation.surface: A measurement for a route that circles one way only.
explanation.walkthrough: A rod, pole or perch is an old British unit of length.
explanation.definitionFit: A road is a way or route, as in Appian Way or roadway.

clue.text: Fish see reflection over lake

indicators.note: a reflection shows a mirror image, so the word appears backwards
in this down entry the reversed word is laid over the other letter, closing round it

parts.note: taken as written
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Fish glimpse their reflection on the surface of a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The lake letter ends up inside the reversed word rather than above it, so 'over' is loose here.
explanation.definitionFit: Eels are long snake-like fish found in rivers and the sea.

clue.text: Plastic switch needed for telephony

indicators.note: to switch letters is to swap them about into another order

parts.note: nine letters used as fodder

explanation.surface: Plastic components and a switch are required for telephone systems.
explanation.walkthrough: Plastic looks like an anagram signal, but it is the definition; switch does that job.
explanation.definitionFit: Polythene, or polyethylene, is the most common plastic, used for bags and wrapping.

clue.text: A star of professional golf

indicators.note: the answer is made of letters taken from the words that follow

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A leading player on the professional golf tour.
explanation.walkthrough: A star of golf suggests a famous player; here it is a real star.
explanation.definitionFit: Algol is the famous variable star in Perseus, known as the Demon Star.
